slides.title: Use your words
slides.text: Tell people how you feel with words. Say 'I'm sad my tower fell' so they can help.

slides.title: Listening matters too
slides.text: Listening is just as important as talking. Look at your friend and hear their story.

slides.title: "Please" and "thank you"
slides.text: Say 'please' when you ask for something. Say 'thank you' when someone helps you.

slides.title: Asking for help
slides.text: Asking for help is smart, not silly. Say 'can you help me, please?' if you're stuck.

slides.title: Your face says a lot too
slides.text: Your face can send a message too. A smile can show you feel happy.

slides.title: Taking turns talking
slides.text: Wait for your turn to talk. Don't interrupt when someone else is talking.

slides.title: Naming your feelings
slides.text: Words like happy, sad, and mad name your feelings. Say 'I feel mad' so people know why.

slides.title: Showing what you mean
slides.text: You can show what you mean too. Point at the fan if you don't know its name.

slides.title: Saying sorry
slides.text: Say sorry when you hurt someone. Say 'I'm sorry I broke your tower.'

slides.title: Your voice has a tone
slides.text: Your voice can sound happy or mad. A soft voice feels kinder than a loud one.

slides.title: It's okay to ask questions
slides.text: It's okay to say 'I don't understand.' Ask 'what do you mean?' if you're not sure.

slides.title: Talking on the phone
slides.text: A phone call is different from talking face to face. Speak clearly so the other person can hear you.

quiz.question: What helps people understand how you feel?
choices: Using your words to say it
Never saying anything at all
quiz.explanation: Putting feelings into words helps others understand and help you.

quiz.question: Is listening as important as talking?
choices: Yes, listening matters too
No, only talking matters
quiz.explanation: Listening is just as important as talking.

quiz.question: When should you say "please"?
choices: When you're asking for something
Only on your birthday
quiz.explanation: "Please" is a polite way to ask for something.

quiz.question: You can't reach a toy on a high shelf. What should you do?
choices: Ask for help with your words
Never tell anyone
quiz.explanation: Asking for help is a smart, strong choice.

quiz.question: Can your face send a message without words?
choices: Yes, like a smile or a frown
No, only words send messages
quiz.explanation: Facial expressions communicate feelings even before you say a word.

quiz.question: What do words like "happy" and "sad" help you do?
choices: Name your feelings
Nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Feeling words help you tell someone what's going on inside you.

quiz.question: You don't know a word. What else can help you show what you mean?
choices: Pointing or drawing
Nothing can help
quiz.explanation: Showing what you mean helps when words are hard to find.

quiz.question: You broke your friend's toy by accident. What should you say?
choices: I'm sorry
Nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Saying sorry helps fix a hurt feeling.

quiz.question: Which voice sounds kinder?
choices: A soft, calm voice
A loud, yelling voice
quiz.explanation: A soft voice feels kinder than a loud one.

quiz.question: You don't understand what someone said. What should you do?
choices: Ask 'what do you mean?'
Just nod and stay confused
quiz.explanation: Asking questions helps you understand better.

slides.title: What is active listening?
slides.text: Active listening means paying close attention to the person who is talking. If a friend explains a new game, nod along and ask a question instead of waiting for your turn.

slides.title: Body language basics
slides.text: Crossed arms, a big smile, or looking away all send a message without any words. If a friend says 'I'm fine' but won't look at you, their body might be telling you something different.

slides.title: Taking turns in conversation
slides.text: A good conversation feels like a back-and-forth game of catch, not one person talking the whole time. If you talk about your weekend for five minutes straight, ask your friend about theirs too.

slides.title: Disagreeing politely
slides.text: You can disagree with someone without being mean about it. If a friend loved a movie you didn't, saying 'I see it differently' keeps things friendly instead of starting an argument.

slides.title: Asking clarifying questions
slides.text: If you don't understand something, it's smarter to ask than to pretend you understood. When a teacher explains a math step too fast, asking 'can you show that again?' gets you real help.

slides.title: Written vs. spoken words
slides.text: Writing a message can feel very different from saying the same words out loud. Texting just 'fine' can sound annoyed, even though saying it with a smile would sound totally different.

slides.title: Checking in on feelings
slides.text: Asking a friend 'are you okay?' shows you notice more than just their words. If a friend seems quiet at lunch and isn't smiling, checking in shows you care.

slides.title: Talking on the phone
slides.text: On a phone call, you can't see the other person's face, so your voice has to do more work. Speaking clearly and asking 'does that make sense?' matters even more than it does in person.

slides.title: Comforting a sad friend
slides.text: Sometimes a friend doesn't need advice right away, just someone to listen. If a friend's pet is sick, saying 'that sounds really hard' can help more than jumping straight to advice.

slides.title: Using your tone of voice
slides.text: The same words can sound totally different depending on your tone of voice. Saying 'okay' in a flat, annoyed voice feels very different from saying it with a smile.

slides.title: Saying sorry the right way
slides.text: A good apology names what you did and how it might have made someone feel. Saying 'I'm sorry I broke your model, that must have been frustrating' means more than just 'sorry.'

slides.title: Giving feedback kindly
slides.text: When you tell a friend how to improve something, focus on the specific thing, not the whole person. Saying 'maybe add more color here' helps more than just saying 'this isn't very good.'

slides.title: Texting vs. talking in person
slides.text: A quick text can't show your face or the tone in your voice. Save texts for simple stuff, and save talking in person for things that really matter.

quiz.question: What is "active listening"?
choices: Really paying attention instead of just waiting to talk
Talking as much as possible
quiz.explanation: Active listening means genuinely focusing on what the other person is saying.

quiz.question: A friend says "I'm fine" with crossed arms and won't look at you. What might their body language suggest?
choices: They might not actually be fine
Body language never means anything
quiz.explanation: Body language often communicates feelings just as clearly as words do.

quiz.question: What does a good conversation feel like?
choices: A back-and-forth, like a game of catch
One person talking the whole time
quiz.explanation: Good conversations involve both people talking and listening in turn.

quiz.question: A friend loved a movie you didn't. How can you disagree politely?
choices: Say something like "I see it differently"
Yell that they're wrong
quiz.explanation: Polite disagreement keeps the conversation respectful, even with different opinions.

quiz.question: A teacher explains a math step quickly and you're lost. What's smart to do?
choices: Ask them to explain again
Pretend you understood anyway
quiz.explanation: Asking for clarification helps you actually understand, instead of guessing.

quiz.question: Why can texting "fine" sound more annoyed than saying it out loud with a smile?
choices: Tone can be easy to misread in writing
Writing always sounds exactly like talking
quiz.explanation: Written messages can lose tone easily, which is why misunderstandings happen in texts.

quiz.question: Why does speaking clearly matter more on a phone call?
choices: You can't see the other person's face for extra clues
It matters less than in person
quiz.explanation: Without facial expressions, your voice has to carry the whole message.

quiz.question: A friend's pet is sick and they're upset. What often helps most, right away?
choices: Sitting with them and saying "that sounds hard"
A long list of advice immediately
quiz.explanation: Being heard and understood often matters more at first than getting advice.

quiz.question: Which sounds friendlier: saying "okay" with a flat voice or saying it with a smile?
choices: Saying it with a smile
They always sound the same
quiz.explanation: Tone of voice changes how the same words feel.

quiz.question: What makes an apology feel more real?
choices: Naming what happened and how it felt
Just saying the word "sorry" quickly
quiz.explanation: A good apology shows you understand how your actions affected someone.

quiz.question: When should you talk in person instead of texting?
choices: When something really matters
Never, texting is always better
quiz.explanation: Texting can't carry tone of voice or facial expressions the way talking in person can.

slides.title: Knowing your audience
slides.text: How you explain something to a younger sibling is different from how you'd explain it to a teacher — good communicators adjust to who they're talking to. For example, explaining a video game's rules to a 5-year-old sibling might use simple words and lots of patience, while explaining the same rules to a teacher for a project might use more precise, detailed language.

slides.title: Persuasive communication
slides.text: Persuading someone works best with clear reasons and evidence, not just repeating what you want louder. For example, asking a parent for a later bedtime by saying "can I stay up later, please, please, please" is much weaker than explaining "I finish my homework by 8, and an extra 30 minutes would let me read before bed" with a real reason behind it.

slides.title: Reading tone in messages
slides.text: A short text like 'fine.' can come across as annoyed even if it wasn't meant that way — being aware of this helps avoid mixed-up messages. For example, texting just "k" in response to a friend's exciting news might come across as dismissive, even if you were just typing quickly and meant nothing by it.

slides.title: Giving feedback kindly
slides.text: Good feedback focuses on the specific thing that could improve, said kindly — not a vague or harsh comment about the person. For example, saying "the intro was a little confusing, maybe start with your main point first" helps a group project partner improve, while "this is bad" just makes them feel criticized without knowing what to fix.

slides.title: Receiving feedback well
slides.text: Hearing feedback about something you did isn't the same as being told you're a bad person — separating the two helps you actually improve. For example, if a teacher says your essay's conclusion needs work, that's feedback about one part of your writing, not a judgment about your intelligence or worth as a person.

slides.title: Resolving a disagreement
slides.text: Calmly explaining your side, actually listening to theirs, and looking for a solution both people can accept usually works better than arguing to 'win.' For example, if you and a sibling disagree about which show to watch, calmly explaining why you want your choice, listening to their reason, and maybe agreeing to alternate shows usually ends better than a shouting match over the remote.

slides.title: Written communication skills
slides.text: A clear, organized message — like a well-written email or message — gets read and understood much more easily than a rushed, jumbled one. For example, a message that says "Hi Coach, I'll miss practice Tuesday for a dentist appointment. See you Thursday!" gets a much faster, clearer response than a rambling message that buries that same information in the middle.

slides.title: Speaking up in a group
slides.text: Sharing your idea in front of a group takes practice. Preparing what you want to say ahead of time makes it feel much less intimidating. For example, jotting down two or three key points before a group discussion means you won't freeze up trying to remember what you wanted to say when it's your turn.

slides.title: Writing a clear message
slides.text: A short, well-organized message — saying exactly what you need and by when — gets a faster, better response than a vague, rambling one. For example, "Can you send me the group project notes by Thursday? I want to start my part this weekend" gets a much clearer response than just "hey, can you send me stuff sometime?"

slides.title: Asking clarifying questions
slides.text: Asking a question when you're confused isn't a weakness — it usually saves everyone time and prevents mistakes later on. For example, saying "just to make sure, do you want this by Friday or next Friday?" takes five seconds and can prevent an entire assignment from being turned in on the wrong day.

slides.title: Apologizing well
slides.text: A real apology names what happened and how it affected the other person, instead of a quick, empty "sorry." For example, saying "I'm sorry I was late and made you wait alone, that wasn't fair to you" shows you actually understand the impact, while a mumbled "sorry" walking past someone often doesn't.

slides.title: Tone of voice matters as much as words
slides.text: The exact same sentence can sound supportive or sarcastic depending on your tone of voice, speed, and volume. For example, saying "sure, whatever you say" can sound genuinely agreeable or completely sarcastic, depending only on how it's said — the words themselves don't change at all.

slides.title: Choosing text, call, or in person
slides.text: Not every message deserves the same format — quick logistics fit a text, but anything emotional or complicated usually goes better as a call or face-to-face talk. For example, texting "running 10 min late" is fine, but resolving a serious argument by text usually leaves too much room for misreading tone.

quiz.question: Why does "knowing your audience" matter?
choices: Good communicators adjust how they explain things to who they're talking to
You should explain everything exactly the same way to everyone
quiz.explanation: Adjusting your explanation to your audience makes communication more effective.

quiz.question: Asking for a later bedtime, which works better: repeating "please, please, please" or explaining a specific reason?
choices: Explaining a specific reason, like homework finishing early
Repeating the same demand louder
quiz.explanation: Solid reasoning tends to persuade far better than volume alone.

quiz.question: Why can texting just "k" in response to exciting news come across as dismissive?
choices: Tone is hard to read without facial expressions or voice
Text messages are always crystal clear
quiz.explanation: Without tone of voice or expression, short texts can come across differently than intended.

quiz.question: Which is more helpful feedback on a group project intro: "this is bad" or "the intro was confusing, try leading with your main point"?
choices: The specific, kind version about the main point
The vague, harsh version
quiz.explanation: Specific, kind feedback is more useful and easier to hear than vague criticism.

quiz.question: A teacher says your essay's conclusion needs work. How can you receive that well?
choices: Separate feedback about the essay from your worth as a person
Assume any feedback means you're a bad person
quiz.explanation: Feedback about what you did isn't a judgment of who you are.

quiz.question: You and a sibling disagree about which show to watch. What usually resolves this better than arguing to "win"?
choices: Listening to the other side and finding a solution both can accept
Talking louder until the other person gives up
quiz.explanation: Genuinely listening and finding common ground resolves disagreements more durably.

quiz.question: What makes speaking up in a group feel less intimidating?
choices: Preparing what you want to say ahead of time
Never thinking about it beforehand
quiz.explanation: Preparation builds confidence before speaking in front of others.

quiz.question: Which message gets a faster, better response: "hey, can you send me stuff sometime?" or a specific ask with a deadline?
choices: The specific one with a clear deadline
The vague one
quiz.explanation: Clarity makes it easy for the reader to know exactly what to do.

quiz.question: Why is asking a clarifying question usually a smart move?
choices: It saves time and prevents mistakes
It makes you look less smart
quiz.explanation: A quick question up front is faster than fixing a mistake later.

quiz.question: What makes an apology feel real instead of empty?
choices: Naming what happened and how it affected the other person
Saying the word 'sorry' as fast as possible
quiz.explanation: A specific apology shows you understand the impact of what happened.

quiz.question: Which kind of message usually goes better as a call or in person instead of a text?
choices: Something emotional or complicated
A quick logistics update like 'running late'
quiz.explanation: Texts are great for simple facts but can easily be misread when the topic is emotional.

slides.title: Public speaking basics
slides.text: Speaking to a group feels easier with preparation: knowing your key points, practicing out loud, and remembering that some nerves are completely normal. For example, practicing a class presentation out loud three times beforehand — even alone in your room — makes an enormous difference in how confident you sound on the actual day.

slides.title: Assertive vs. passive vs. aggressive
slides.text: Assertive communication states your needs clearly and respectfully. Passive avoids saying what you need. Aggressive disregards the other person's feelings entirely. For example, if a group project partner isn't doing their share, saying "I need you to finish your part by Friday so we're not scrambling" is assertive — staying silent and hoping it fixes itself is passive, and yelling "you never do anything" is aggressive.

slides.title: Conflict resolution
slides.text: Resolving conflict well usually means naming the real issue calmly, listening fully to the other side, and working toward a solution instead of assigning blame. For example, instead of saying "you always ignore me," naming the specific issue — "I felt left out when the group made plans without me" — opens the door to an actual conversation instead of a defensive reaction.

slides.title: Professional communication
slides.text: A clear subject line, a polite tone, and getting to the point efficiently make emails and messages far more effective in school or work settings. For example, an email titled "Question about Friday's assignment deadline" with two clear sentences gets answered far faster than one titled "hi" with a long, unfocused paragraph.

slides.title: Digital communication etiquette
slides.text: What you'd never say to someone's face shouldn't be said online either — screenshots and messages tend to stick around far longer than a spoken conversation. For example, a harsh comment typed in frustration can be screenshotted and shared long after you've cooled down and moved past the moment — something a spoken argument doesn't leave behind.

slides.title: Listening for understanding, not rebuttal
slides.text: Truly listening means trying to understand the other person's point, not just waiting for your turn to argue back. For example, in a disagreement about curfew, really listening to why a parent is worried (not just waiting to counter-argue) might reveal a specific concern you could actually address directly.

slides.title: Communicating across differences
slides.text: People from different backgrounds may communicate in different styles — being aware of this helps avoid misreading someone's tone or intent. For example, someone raised in a culture that values indirect communication might phrase a disagreement much more softly than someone used to being very direct — neither is wrong, but misreading the difference can cause unnecessary friction.

slides.title: Nonverbal cues under pressure
slides.text: In a tense conversation, tone of voice and body language often carry as much meaning as the actual words being said. For example, saying "I'm not mad" through gritted teeth and crossed arms sends a very different message than the actual words — the tone and body language often reveal more truth than the sentence itself.

slides.title: Communicating across cultures online
slides.text: Humor, directness, and how formal a message should be all vary a lot between cultures — a message that reads as friendly in one context can read as blunt or confusing in another. For example, a very short, direct message that feels efficient and normal in one culture's messaging style might come across as cold or rude to someone from a culture where messages are typically warmer and more elaborate.

slides.title: Introducing yourself professionally
slides.text: A short, confident self-introduction — your name, what you're interested in, and why you're reaching out — makes a strong first impression in interviews or networking. For example, "Hi, I'm Jordan, a junior interested in environmental science, and I'm reaching out because I'd love to learn more about your research" makes a far stronger first impression than a vague, rambling introduction.

slides.title: Giving and receiving feedback like a pro
slides.text: Good feedback is specific and focused on the work, not a vague judgment of the person delivering or receiving it. For example, telling a coworker "the report's third section repeats the intro, maybe cut it" is more useful than "this needs work," and receiving similar feedback without getting defensive is just as important a skill.

slides.title: Apologizing without over-explaining
slides.text: A strong apology takes responsibility clearly and briefly, without piling on excuses that shift the blame elsewhere. For example, "I'm sorry I missed the deadline, I should have asked for help sooner" lands better than a long explanation of everything that went wrong that week.

slides.title: Reading the room
slides.text: The same joke or comment can land differently depending on the mood of the room, so paying attention to context matters as much as what you actually say. For example, a sarcastic joke that gets laughs at a casual hangout might fall flat or seem rude during a serious team meeting.

slides.title: Delivering difficult news
slides.text: Sharing bad news clearly and with empathy — without burying it in vague language — respects the other person more than softening it so much it's confusing. For example, saying "I won't be able to finish this by Friday, I need two more days" is more respectful than a vague message that leaves someone guessing until the deadline passes.

quiz.question: A group partner isn't doing their share. Which response is assertive?
choices: "I need you to finish your part by Friday"
Staying silent and hoping it fixes itself
quiz.explanation: Assertive communication is respectful and clear — different from passive or aggressive styles.

quiz.question: What usually helps resolve a conflict well?
choices: Naming the real issue calmly and listening to the other side
Assigning blame as fast as possible
quiz.explanation: Calm, issue-focused conversation resolves conflict more effectively than blame.

quiz.question: Which email subject line is more effective: "hi" or "Question about Friday's assignment deadline"?
choices: "Question about Friday's assignment deadline"
"hi"
quiz.explanation: Clarity and politeness make professional messages easier to act on.

quiz.question: Why does digital communication etiquette matter?
choices: Online messages can stick around and spread much longer than spoken words
Nothing online is ever remembered
quiz.explanation: Digital messages can be screenshotted and shared long after they were sent.

quiz.question: "Listening for understanding, not rebuttal" means what?
choices: Trying to understand the other person, not just planning your comeback
Waiting silently only so you can argue back harder
quiz.explanation: Real listening means genuinely trying to understand, not just preparing a rebuttal.

quiz.question: Someone says "I'm not mad" through gritted teeth with crossed arms. What carries more meaning here?
choices: Tone of voice and body language
Nothing besides the literal words used
quiz.explanation: Nonverbal cues frequently communicate as much as, or more than, the words alone.

quiz.question: Why might people from different backgrounds communicate differently?
choices: Communication styles can vary by culture and background
Everyone communicates in exactly the same way everywhere
quiz.explanation: Being aware that communication styles vary helps avoid misreading someone's intent.

quiz.question: Why can a short, direct message read as blunt to someone from a different culture?
choices: Norms around tone and directness vary across cultures
Every culture communicates in exactly the same way
quiz.explanation: Being mindful of cultural differences in tone helps avoid unintended misunderstandings.

quiz.question: What makes a strong professional self-introduction?
choices: Your name, your interest, and why you're reaching out, kept short
A long, unfocused life story
quiz.explanation: A brief, confident introduction makes a stronger first impression than a rambling one.

quiz.question: What makes feedback most useful?
choices: Being specific about the work, not the person
Being vague so it doesn't hurt feelings
quiz.explanation: Specific, work-focused feedback is easier to act on than a vague judgment.

quiz.question: Which apology is stronger: a brief, direct one or a long list of excuses?
choices: A brief, direct one that takes responsibility
A long explanation of everything that went wrong
quiz.explanation: Taking responsibility clearly, without piling on excuses, lands better than over-explaining.

quiz.question: Why does "reading the room" matter in communication?
choices: The same words can land differently depending on the setting
Context never changes how a comment is received
quiz.explanation: Paying attention to mood and setting helps you judge what will land well.
